title: How Is Marijuana Vaping Portrayed on YouTube? Content, Features, Popularity and Retransmission of Vaping Marijuana YouTube Videos
screen_reason: Content analysis of 214 marijuana-vaping YouTube videos in which the presence/absence of misinformation and of misleading information was explicitly coded by trained coders against an expert-consensus reference standard, with reliability reported. The Results give both shares against the 214-video denominator: 8 videos (3.7%) contained misinformation and 24 (11.2%) contained misleading information. Those are CONTENT estimates. The paper's aim (portrayal, popularity, retransmission) is different, but the descriptive shares are reported, so it is eligible.

estimates.country: Not stated (YouTube archive; US-based authors and US framing)
estimates.date: videos published July 2014 - June 2015 (archive searched for that window)
estimates.measure_type: % of marijuana-vaping YouTube videos containing misinformation (claim incorrect by expert consensus)
estimates.denominator: 214 vaping-marijuana YouTube videos (from 469 retrieved by keyword search of the July 2014-June 2015 archive, after removing 171 deleted by users, 4 duplicates, 9 unrelated and 71 about only marijuana or only e-cigarettes)
estimates.definition: Video coded as containing misinformation if it presented information currently considered incorrect by expert consensus (example given: "Marijuana is legal in all 50 states"); the authors describe this as a strict/conservative definition requiring information demonstrably inconsistent with credible sources such as NIDA.
estimates.misinfo_def: "misinformation operationalized as the information currently considered to be incorrect by expert consensus (e.g., 'Marijuana is legal in all 50 states')"
estimates.source_quote: Eight (3.7%) and 24 videos (11.2%) included misinformation or misleading information respectively
estimates.page_loc: Results, Descriptive Statistics, p. 7 of the author manuscript
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three coders (two study designers plus one naive coder blind to the research questions); multi-stage reliability protocol with training on 25 clips and re-checks at the midpoint and near the end; Krippendorff's alpha across the three stages ranged from .70 to 1.00 (per-variable alpha for the misinformation item is not broken out). Reference standard: expert consensus / credible sources such as NIDA.
estimates.moderator_quote: To retrieve vaping marijuana YouTube videos, we used a series of keywords to search the title and descriptions of YouTube archive from July 2014 through June 2015, and originally retrieved 469 videos, among which 171 had been removed by users when we designed the study. After deduplication (n = 4) and excluding those that are not related to either marijuana or vaping (n = 9) and those that related to only marijuana or e-cigarettes (n = 71), we obtained a final sample of 214 videos.
estimates.notes: 8/214 = 3.7%, matching the printed value. The authors themselves attribute the low figure to the strict definition and to the thin evidence base on vaping marijuana: "very few instances of misinformation were identified due to our strict definition of misinformation, where information must be demonstrably inconsistent with information from credible sources (such as NIDA). Due to limited scientific data on vaping marijuana's health effects, there is little officially endorsed information to be refuted." Videos over five minutes were coded on their first five minutes only, so misinformation later in long videos could be missed. denom_selection left blank: this is a keyword census of the archive window, not a top-N or most-viewed set.

estimates.country: Not stated (YouTube archive; US-based authors and US framing)
estimates.date: videos published July 2014 - June 2015 (archive searched for that window)
estimates.measure_type: % of marijuana-vaping YouTube videos containing misleading information (not explicitly false but liable to produce inaccurate inferences)
estimates.denominator: 214 vaping-marijuana YouTube videos (same corpus as the misinformation row)
estimates.definition: Video coded as containing misleading information if it presented information that is not explicitly false, or for which scientific evidence to prove it incorrect is lacking, but which may result in making inaccurate inferences (example given: "CBD oil will not get you high").
estimates.misinfo_def: "misleading information as the information that is not explicitly false, or there is a lack of scientific evidence to prove it as incorrect, but may result in making inaccurate inferences (e.g., 'CBD oil will not get you high')"
estimates.source_quote: Eight (3.7%) and 24 videos (11.2%) included misinformation or misleading information respectively
estimates.page_loc: Results, Descriptive Statistics, p. 7 of the author manuscript
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same three-coder protocol and multi-stage Krippendorff's alpha (.70-1.00) as the misinformation row; reference standard is expert consensus / credible sources, with the misleading category covering claims not provably false but liable to mislead.
estimates.moderator_quote: We also coded the presence/absence of misinformation or misleading information, with misinformation operationalized as the information currently considered to be incorrect by expert consensus ... while misleading information as the information that is not explicitly false ... but may result in making inaccurate inferences.
estimates.notes: definition_variant=true: this is the broader veracity band on the SAME 214-video corpus as the 3.7% misinformation row, so the two must not be treated as independent estimates, and their sum (32 videos, 15.0%) is a cross-category sum and is NOT reported per R8. Judgement call for the adjudicator: kept as CONTENT rather than QUALITY because the coding is an explicit misleading/false veracity judgement against an expert reference standard, not a completeness or quality score; the residual worry is that the definition covers claims merely lacking evidence, so an item that turns out true could carry the label.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Valence is not a veracity measure and was not extracted: "Videos in our sample were predominantly 'pro' (98.1%), while only 0.5% were 'neutral' and 1.4% were 'anti' to vaping marijuana." Same for genre shares (user-sharing 34.1%, product review 23.4%, advertisement 21.0%, instructional 8.9%), appeals (social 18.7%, humour 7.0%, fear 0.9%), brand mentions (40.1%) and the demographic shares of on-screen characters - all content features, not falsity. (2) Promotional/warning-argument frequencies are in Table 3, which the text extraction does not render; if the review ever codes 'unsupported health claims' as misinformation, that table would need the PDF. (3) No exposure/sharing estimate is poolable: views, shares, comments, likes and dislikes are reported only as means and ranges (e.g. views M = 12,192.24, shares M = 20.74), and the relationship between misleading information and viewership is reported as a coefficient (beta = .15, p < .05), not as a share of views going to misleading videos. (4) The combined 'any misinformation or misleading information' figure is not printed and was not computed (cross-category sum, forbidden by R8). (5) Country is never stated; the corpus is the global YouTube archive filtered by English-language keywords, hence country_norm Global. (6) Survivorship caveat: 171 of the 469 originally retrieved videos had already been removed by users before coding, so the denominator is the surviving subset. (7) Per-variable inter-coder reliability for the misinformation/misleading items is not reported separately, only the .70-1.00 range across all coded variables.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Sampling frame: keyword search (90 e-cigarette terms filtered by 15 marijuana terms) over titles and descriptions of the YouTube archive July 2014-June 2015; 469 videos retrieved, 171 already user-deleted, minus 4 duplicates, 9 unrelated and 71 single-topic videos, leaving n = 214. No response rate applies. Coding by three coders (two designers plus one naive coder blind to the research questions) with a multi-stage reliability protocol: 25 videos co-coded (10 for training), reliability recalculated at the midpoint and again with 15 videos left; Krippendorff's alpha .70 to 1.00 across stages, not broken out per variable. Videos shorter than five minutes were viewed entirely, longer ones only for their first five minutes. Misinformation defined strictly against expert consensus/NIDA; a separate broader 'misleading information' category was coded. Details of the specific misinformation instances were not published ("available upon request").
rob.item6_quote: We also coded the presence/absence of misinformation or misleading information, with misinformation operationalized as the information currently considered to be incorrect by expert consensus (e.g., "Marijuana is legal in all 50 states"), while misleading information as the information that is not explicitly false, or there is a lack of scientific evidence to prove it as incorrect, but may result in making inaccurate inferences (e.g., "CBD oil will not get you high").
rob.item10_quote: Eight (3.7%) and 24 videos (11.2%) included misinformation or misleading information respectively
